client: I've been spiraling ever since I failed that biochemistry exam last semester. I keep obsessing over how it might ruin my chances of keeping my pre-med scholarship, and I can't stop imagining worst-case scenarios where I flunk out completely. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - the fear just feels so overwhelming and real.
therapist: I hear how deeply this exam failure is affecting you—the worry about your scholarship and future feels all-consuming right now. While your words express a lot of fear, I notice your voice sounds a bit more subdued—almost like part of you feels drained by these thoughts. Would it help to explore how these "worst-case scenario" thoughts might be affecting your energy and motivation day-to-day?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
It does feel draining, like I'm stuck in this loop of imagining all the ways this could ruin everything. I keep picturing having to drop out of school, disappointing my parents... but at the same time, part of me knows I'm probably catastrophizing. It's just hard to stop when the consequences feel so real.  

I don't know if exploring the thoughts will help—they already take up so much space in my head. What if digging into them just makes the anxiety worse?
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between recognizing these thoughts might be exaggerated and feeling paralyzed by how believable they seem—that tension itself must be exhausting. When you say "they take up so much space," I wonder if you've noticed specific times of day when these thoughts feel louder or quieter?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
It's definitely worse in the mornings when I first wake up. My mind immediately starts racing with all the things that could go wrong that day. By afternoon it's a little better, but then at night the thoughts come back even stronger when I'm trying to sleep. 

I don't know if it's exhaustion making the thoughts feel louder at night, or just being alone with them. Either way, it feels like they control my whole day from start to finish.
therapist: The way these thoughts seem to have their own daily rhythm—intense in mornings and nights, slightly easing in afternoons—sounds incredibly difficult to live with. I notice when you describe this pattern, your voice sounds wearier than your words might suggest—like the constant back-and-forth is wearing you down. Have you noticed anything different about the afternoons when the thoughts ease slightly—what's happening in those moments that might create even that small relief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
Honestly, I don't feel like the afternoons are any better—just less exhausting because I'm distracted. At work, I'm forced to focus on spreadsheets and emails, but the second I finish a task, the thoughts come rushing back. It's not real relief, just postponing the anxiety until I'm alone with my thoughts again.  

And even the distraction feels awful lately—like I'm just going through motions while my brain screams in the background. I've tried leaning into the afternoon "breaks," but it makes me angrier when the anxiety returns because I hoped it might actually stay gone this time.
therapist:
It sounds like even the temporary distractions aren't giving you the respite you hoped for—instead leaving you feeling almost betrayed when the anxiety returns. The way you describe your brain "screaming in the background" while you work suggests this is more than just worry—it's like your mind won't let you rest even during mundane tasks. 

I notice you mentioned anger when the anxiety resurfaces—could you tell me more about what that anger feels like in those moments? Is it directed at yourself, the situation, or something else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: The anger feels like frustration boiling up because I can't escape my own thoughts. It's mostly directed at myself—like I should be able to handle this better, but I can't. Sometimes it feels unfair, like why can't I just have a moment of peace without my brain dragging me back into this spiral?
therapist:
You're carrying so much frustration—not just about the thoughts themselves, but about feeling trapped by them, and then being frustrated with yourself for feeling trapped. That double layer sounds exhausting. I notice when you describe this, your voice speeds up but also quiets, almost like you're both racing through these feelings and trying to shrink from them at the same time. 

When you say "why can't I just have a moment of peace," it makes me wonder: if a friend were going through this, would you judge them as harshly as you're judging yourself right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I never thought about it that way—how I'd probably be way kinder to a friend than I am to myself. But even knowing that, it's hard to stop the self-judgment. The frustration just feels automatic, like my brain's stuck in this loop I can't control. 

And yeah, it is exhausting. Sometimes I notice my shoulders are tense for hours because I'm mentally beating myself up over things that probably wouldn't even bother me if someone else did them. But knowing that doesn't make the feelings stop.
therapist:
It's striking how aware you are of this pattern—noticing the physical tension, recognizing the double standard in how you treat others versus yourself—yet that awareness alone hasn't been enough to break the cycle. The way you describe it as "automatic" makes me think these reactions have become almost reflexive for you. 

When you notice your shoulders tensing up during these moments, has there ever been a time when you were able to interrupt that physical reaction, even briefly? I'm curious what that might have looked like.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I remember one time last week when I caught myself tensing up during a work meeting, and I tried to take a deep breath. But then I immediately thought "I shouldn't need to do this - other people just handle stress normally," and the tension came back even worse. It's frustrating because even when I notice it, the self-judgment makes it harder to relax. 

Sometimes I wonder if trying to change these reactions just makes me focus on them more. Like I'm hyper-aware of every little tension in my body now, and that awareness itself becomes stressful.
therapist:
That moment in the meeting captures such a painful cycle—trying to help yourself with the breath, then the self-criticism undoing any relief, leaving you even more tense. It's like there's no space to just *be* with the stress—it has to immediately become another reason to judge yourself. 

When you say "hyper-aware of every little tension," it makes me wonder—has there ever been a time when noticing those sensations *didn't* spiral into judgment? Even if just for a fleeting moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
Hmm, I guess there was one time last week when I noticed my shoulders were tight during a coffee break, and for like two seconds I just stretched them out without overthinking it. But then immediately my brain went "See? You're always tense, you can't even relax for five minutes." 

It's like my body awareness is always a trap—either I don't notice the tension until it's overwhelming, or when I do notice, it just becomes proof that I'm failing at handling stress.
therapist:
That small moment of just stretching without overthinking—before the judgment crept in—sounds like an important glimpse of what could be possible. I notice when you describe this, your voice speeds up like you're rushing past that tiny moment of relief to get back to the familiar self-criticism. 

What do you think it would feel like if, just for that coffee break, you'd been able to stay with that stretch for five more seconds before the judgment showed up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I don't know... those few seconds of just stretching did feel kind of nice, but it's like my brain immediately ruins it by saying "you shouldn't need breaks" or "this won't fix anything." Staying with it longer sounds scary because then the crash back into anxiety feels even worse. Like I'm just setting myself up for disappointment.
therapist:
It sounds like even the possibility of brief relief comes with fear—that letting yourself feel it momentarily will make the return to anxiety more painful. There's something so human in that struggle—wanting the break, yet bracing against it because the contrast afterward stings. 

When you describe those few seconds of just stretching, your voice lifts slightly—like part of you recognizes how rare and valuable those uncomplicated moments are. What would it feel like to acknowledge that part, even if the critic tries to drown it out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I do notice those little moments, but it's like my brain immediately panics and says "Don't get used to this." The relief feels dangerous somehow, like if I enjoy it too much, the crash back into anxiety will be even worse. I want to hold onto those good seconds longer, but I don't know how to do that without feeling like I'm setting myself up for disappointment.
therapist:
It sounds like those moments of relief feel almost fragile—like they might shatter if you hold onto them too long. The way you describe wanting to stay with them but fearing the "crash" afterward suggests a kind of protective instinct, as if your brain is trying to shield you from disappointment by staying guarded. 

What do you think would happen if, just for one moment, you let yourself linger in that stretch or breath without worrying about what comes next—not trying to make it last, just letting it be what it is?
